units.title: Kindergarten: Forces and Interactions: Pushes and Pulls

topics.title: Forces and Interactions: Pushes and Pulls

outcomes.text: Investigate how stronger or weaker pushes and pulls, and different directions, change how an object moves.
Use test data to judge whether a design changes the speed or direction of an object with a push or pull.

units.title: Kindergarten: Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems: Animals, Plants, and Their Environment

topics.title: Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems: Animals, Plants, and Their Environment

outcomes.text: Observe plants and animals, including people, and describe patterns in what they need to survive.
Argue with evidence that plants and animals change their environment to meet their needs.
Use a model to show how what plants and animals need relates to the places where they live.
Share ideas for lessening how people harm land, water, air and living things nearby.
Observe how sunlight warms the surface of the Earth.
Design and build a structure that reduces the warming effect of sunlight on a place.
Observe and share local weather to describe how it changes over time.
Ask questions about why we forecast weather and how that helps people prepare for severe weather.
Ask questions and gather information about something people want to change to define a simple solvable problem.
Make a sketch, drawing or model showing how an object's shape helps it solve a problem.
Analyze test data from two objects solving the same problem to compare strengths and weaknesses.
Investigate showing that vibrating things make sound and sound makes things vibrate.
Observe to explain that objects can be seen only when light shines on them.
Test what happens when different materials are placed in a beam of light.
Design and build a device that uses light or sound to send messages over a distance.

units.title: Grade 1: Structure, Function, and Information Processing

outcomes.text: Design a solution to a human problem by copying how plants or animals use external body parts to survive.
Use texts and media to find behavior patterns of parents and young that help the young survive.
Observe to show that young plants and animals resemble, but are not identical to, their parents.

units.title: Grade 1: Space Systems: Patterns and Cycles

outcomes.text: Observe the sun, moon and stars and describe patterns that can be predicted.
Observe through the year to link the amount of daylight to the season.

units.title: Grade 2: Structure and Properties of Matter

outcomes.text: Investigate and sort materials by properties you can observe.
Analyze test data to find which materials best suit an intended use.
Observe how an object made from a few pieces can be taken apart and rebuilt as something new.
Argue with evidence that heating or cooling changes some things reversibly and some not.
Investigate whether plants need sunlight and water to grow.
Build a simple model of an animal spreading seeds or pollinating plants.
Observe plants and animals to compare the variety of life in different habitats.

units.title: Grade 2: Earth's Systems: Processes that Shape the Earth

topics.title: Earth's Systems: Processes that Shape the Earth

outcomes.text: Use several sources to show that some Earth events happen quickly and others slowly.
Compare solutions that slow or stop wind or water from reshaping land.
Make a model showing the shapes and kinds of land and water in an area.
Find out where water exists on Earth and that it can be solid or liquid.
Investigate how balanced and unbalanced forces affect an object's motion.
Observe and measure motion to show a pattern can predict future motion.
Ask questions about cause and effect in electric or magnetic interactions between objects not touching.
Define a simple design problem that can be solved using ideas about magnets.
Argue that some animals form groups that help members survive.
Interpret fossil data to show what organisms and environments existed long ago.
Argue with evidence that in one habitat some organisms survive well, some less well, some not at all.
Judge the merit of a solution to problems caused when a changing environment changes which plants and animals live there.

units.title: Grade 3: Inheritance and Variation of Traits: Life Cycles and Traits

topics.title: Inheritance and Variation of Traits: Life Cycles and Traits

outcomes.text: Model that organisms have different life cycles but all share birth, growth, reproduction and death.
Interpret data to show that traits are inherited and vary within a group of similar organisms.
Use evidence to explain that the environment can influence traits.
Explain with evidence how variation among individuals can help survival, finding mates and reproducing.
Show data in tables and graphs to describe typical weather for a season.
Gather and combine information to describe climates in different regions.
Judge the merit of a design that reduces the effects of a weather-related hazard.
Define a design problem with success criteria and limits on materials, time or cost.
Generate and compare solutions by how well they meet the criteria and constraints.
Plan fair tests with controlled variables to find what in a prototype to improve.
Use evidence to explain how an object's speed relates to its energy.
Observe that energy moves from place to place by sound, light, heat and electric current.
Ask questions and predict energy changes when objects collide.
Design, test and refine a device that changes energy from one form to another.
Combine information to show energy and fuels come from natural resources and affect the environment.
Model waves by amplitude and wavelength and show that waves can move objects.
Generate and compare solutions that use patterns to send information.

units.title: Grade 4: Structure, Function, and Information Processing

outcomes.text: Model how light reflecting off objects and entering the eye lets us see.
Argue that plants and animals have internal and external structures that support survival, growth, behavior and reproduction.
Model how animals take in information with senses, process it in the brain and respond.

units.title: Grade 4: Earth's Systems: Processes that Shape the Earth

topics.title: Earth's Systems: Processes that Shape the Earth

outcomes.text: Use patterns in rock layers and fossils as evidence of how a landscape changed over time.
Observe or measure the effects of weathering and the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind or plants.
Interpret map data to describe patterns in Earth's features.
Generate and compare solutions to reduce the impact of natural Earth processes on people.

units.title: Grade 5: Structure and Properties of Matter

outcomes.text: Model that matter is made of particles too small to see.
Measure and graph to show total weight of matter is conserved when heating, cooling or mixing.
Measure and observe to identify materials from their properties.
Investigate whether mixing substances makes new substances.

units.title: Grade 5: Matter and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems

topics.title: Matter and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems

subtopics.title: Food energy comes from the sun

outcomes.text: Use models to show energy in animals' food was once energy from the sun.
Argue that plants get materials for growth mainly from air and water.
Model how matter moves among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment.
Model with an example how the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere interact.
Describe and graph amounts of salt water and fresh water to show how Earth's water is distributed.
Gather information on how communities use science to protect Earth's resources and environment.

units.title: Grade 5: Space Systems: Stars and the Solar System

topics.title: Space Systems: Stars and the Solar System

outcomes.text: Argue that Earth's gravity pulls objects downward.
Argue that the sun looks brighter than other stars because it is closer.
Graph patterns of shadow changes, day and night, and seasonal stars.

units.title: Middle School: Structure and Properties of Matter

outcomes.text: Build models showing the atoms that make up simple molecules and extended structures.
Gather information showing synthetic materials come from natural resources and affect society.
Model how particle motion, temperature and state of a pure substance change when heat is added or removed.
Analyze data on substances before and after interacting to decide if a reaction occurred.
Model that the number of atoms stays the same in a reaction, so mass is conserved.
Design, test and modify a device that releases or absorbs heat through a chemical process.
Apply Newton's third law to design a solution for two colliding objects.
Plan an investigation showing that motion change depends on the net force and the object's mass.
Ask questions about data to find what affects the strength of electric and magnetic forces.
Argue with evidence that gravity is attractive and depends on the interacting masses.
Investigate and evaluate the design to show fields exist between objects that exert forces without touching.
Graph data to describe how kinetic energy relates to an object's mass and speed.
Model how changing the arrangement of objects interacting at a distance stores different potential energy.
Design, build and test a device that minimizes or maximizes thermal energy transfer.
Plan an investigation of how energy transferred, type of matter and mass affect temperature change.
Argue that when an object's kinetic energy changes, energy is transferred to or from it.

units.title: Middle School: Waves and Electromagnetic Radiation

outcomes.text: Use mathematical representations of a simple wave model relating amplitude to energy.
Model how waves are reflected, absorbed or transmitted through materials.
Support the claim that digitized signals are more reliable than analog for sending information.

units.title: Middle School: Structure, Function, and Information Processing

subtopics.title: Cells as the unit of life

outcomes.text: Investigate to show living things are made of one cell or many cells of different types.
Model the function of a cell as a whole and how its parts contribute.
Argue that the body is a system of interacting subsystems made of groups of cells.
Gather information that sensory receptors respond to stimuli by sending messages to the brain for behavior or memory.

units.title: Middle School: Matter and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems

topics.title: Matter and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems

outcomes.text: Explain with evidence photosynthesis's role in cycling matter and moving energy into and out of organisms.
Model how food is rearranged by chemical reactions into new molecules that support growth or release energy.
Interpret data on how resource availability affects organisms and populations in an ecosystem.
Model the cycling of matter and flow of energy among living and nonliving ecosystem parts.
Argue with evidence that changes to an ecosystem's physical or biological parts affect populations.

units.title: Middle School: Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems

outcomes.text: Explain and predict patterns of interactions among organisms across ecosystems.
Evaluate competing designs for maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem services.

units.title: Middle School: Growth, Development, and Reproduction of Organisms

topics.title: Growth, Development, and Reproduction of Organisms

outcomes.text: Argue how animal behaviors and plant structures affect the chance of successful reproduction.
Explain with evidence how environmental and genetic factors affect organism growth.
Model why gene changes on chromosomes can cause harmful, beneficial or neutral effects on proteins and the organism.
Model why asexual reproduction gives identical offspring while sexual reproduction gives variation.
Gather information on technologies that changed how people influence inheritance of desired traits.

units.title: Middle School: Natural Selection and Adaptations

outcomes.text: Interpret fossil record data showing the existence, diversity, extinction and change of life over time.
Explain anatomical similarities and differences among modern and fossil organisms to infer relationships.
Compare pictures of embryonic development across species to find relationships hidden in adult anatomy.
Explain how genetic variation of traits makes some individuals more likely to survive and reproduce.
Use mathematical representations to explain how natural selection raises or lowers traits in populations over time.
Model the Earth-sun-moon system to explain lunar phases, eclipses and seasons.
Model the role of gravity in motions within galaxies and the solar system.
Interpret data to find scale properties of solar system objects.
Explain, using rock strata, how the geologic time scale organizes Earth's 4.6-billion-year history.
Explain with evidence how geoscience processes changed Earth's surface at different time and size scales.
Interpret fossil, rock, continent-shape and seafloor data as evidence of past plate motions.
Model the cycling of Earth's materials and the energy flow that drives it.
Model water cycling through Earth's systems driven by the sun's energy and gravity.
Explain how past and present geoscience processes caused uneven distribution of minerals, energy and groundwater.
Collect data showing how air-mass motions and interactions change weather.
Model how unequal heating and Earth's rotation drive atmosphere and ocean circulation and regional climates.
Ask questions to clarify evidence for the factors behind the rise in global temperatures.
Interpret natural hazard data to forecast catastrophic events and guide technologies that reduce their effects.
Apply scientific principles to design a method to monitor and reduce a human impact on the environment.
Argue with evidence how more people and greater resource use affect Earth's systems.
Define a design problem's criteria and constraints precisely, considering science and impacts on people and nature.
Evaluate competing design solutions with a systematic process against criteria and constraints.
Analyze test data to find the best features of several solutions and combine them into a new design.
Develop a model that generates data for repeated testing and modification toward an optimal design.

units.title: High School: Structure and Properties of Matter

outcomes.text: Use the periodic table and outer-electron patterns to predict relative properties of elements.
Investigate bulk substances to infer the strength of electrical forces between particles.
Model changes in the nucleus and energy released in fission, fusion and radioactive decay.
Communicate why molecular-level structure matters for how designed materials function.
Explain a simple reaction's outcome from outer electron states, periodic trends and chemical property patterns.
Model that energy released or absorbed in a reaction depends on changes in total bond energy.
Explain how temperature or concentration of reacting particles changes reaction rate.
Refine a chemical system design by changing conditions to produce more product at equilibrium.
Use mathematics to support that atoms, and so mass, are conserved in a reaction.
Analyze data supporting that net force, mass and acceleration are related by Newton's second law.
Use mathematics to show a system's total momentum is conserved when there is no net force.
Design, evaluate and refine a device that minimizes the force on an object in a collision.
Use Newton's law of gravitation and Coulomb's law to predict gravitational and electrostatic forces.
Investigate that current makes a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field makes current.
Build a computational model to find an energy change in a system from known energy flows.
Model energy at large scale as motion energy plus energy from relative position of particles.
Design, build and refine a device that converts energy within given constraints.
Investigate that combining components of different temperatures in a closed system evens out energy.
Model two objects interacting through electric or magnetic fields, showing forces and energy changes.

units.title: High School: Waves and Electromagnetic Radiation

outcomes.text: Use mathematics to relate frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in various media.
Evaluate the advantages of transmitting and storing information digitally.

subtopics.title: Wave and particle models of light

outcomes.text: Evaluate claims that electromagnetic radiation is described by wave or particle models, whichever fits better.
Evaluate the validity of published claims about how frequencies of electromagnetic radiation affect matter.
Communicate how devices use wave behavior and wave-matter interactions to send and capture information.
Explain how DNA structure determines protein structure that carries out life functions in specialized cells.
Model the hierarchical organization of interacting systems in multicellular organisms.
Investigate how feedback mechanisms maintain homeostasis.

units.title: High School: Matter and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems

topics.title: Matter and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems

outcomes.text: Model how photosynthesis turns light energy into stored chemical energy.
Explain how carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from sugars combine with other elements to form amino acids and other large molecules.
Model that respiration breaks food and oxygen bonds and forms new compounds, transferring energy.
Explain cycling of matter and flow of energy in aerobic and anaerobic conditions.
Use mathematics to support claims on matter cycling and energy flow among organisms.
Model how photosynthesis and respiration cycle carbon among biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere and geosphere.

units.title: High School: Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems

outcomes.text: Use mathematical or computational representations to explain factors affecting carrying capacity.
Use mathematics to support and revise explanations of factors affecting biodiversity and populations.
Evaluate claims that ecosystem interactions keep numbers stable, but changing conditions can make a new ecosystem.
Design, evaluate and refine a solution that reduces human effects on environment and biodiversity.
Evaluate evidence for how group behavior affects survival and reproduction.
Create or revise a simulation testing a solution that reduces human harm to biodiversity.

units.title: High School: Inheritance and Variation of Traits

outcomes.text: Model how cell division and differentiation produce and maintain complex organisms.
Ask questions about how DNA and chromosomes code instructions for inherited traits.
Defend a claim that variation comes from meiosis, copying errors and environment-caused mutations.
Apply statistics and probability to explain variation and distribution of traits in a population.

units.title: High School: Natural Selection and Evolution

outcomes.text: Communicate how multiple lines of evidence support common ancestry and evolution.
Explain that evolution results from population growth potential, heritable variation, competition and selection.
Use statistics and probability to show advantageous heritable traits become more common.
Explain with evidence how natural selection leads to adaptation of populations.
Evaluate evidence that environmental change can increase some species, create new ones or cause extinctions.
Model the sun's life span and the role of nuclear fusion in releasing its energy.
Explain the Big Bang using light spectra, galaxy motion and the composition of matter.
Communicate how stars produce elements over their life cycle.
Use mathematics to predict the motion of orbiting objects in the solar system.
Evaluate evidence of crust movements and plate tectonics to explain ages of crustal rocks.
Use evidence from ancient Earth materials, meteorites and planetary surfaces to account for Earth's formation.
Model how internal and surface processes at different scales form continental and ocean-floor features.
Analyze data to claim that one change to Earth's surface can cause feedbacks in other systems.
Model Earth's interior to describe cycling of matter by thermal convection.
Investigate water's properties and its effects on Earth materials and surface processes.
Build a quantitative model of carbon cycling among hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere and biosphere.
Argue with evidence that Earth's systems and life coevolved.
Model how changes in energy flow into and out of Earth's systems change climate.
Use geoscience data and climate models to forecast rates of climate change and its impacts.
Explain how natural resources, hazards and climate change have influenced human activity.
Evaluate competing designs for managing energy and mineral resources by cost-benefit ratios.
Create a simulation relating resource management, human population sustainability and biodiversity.
Evaluate or refine technology that reduces human impacts on natural systems.
Use a computational representation to show how human activity modifies relationships among Earth systems.
Analyze a global challenge to set criteria and constraints reflecting societal needs and wants.
Design a solution to a complex problem by splitting it into smaller solvable problems.
Evaluate a solution against prioritized criteria and trade-offs such as cost, safety, reliability and aesthetics.
Use a computer simulation to model the impact of proposed solutions on interacting systems.
